source_text: Venio nunc ad eam quae percipitur ex tactu uoluptatem: qui sensus est quidem totius corporis. sed ego non de ornamentis ac uestibus, sed de sola libidine dicendum mihi puto, quae maxime coercenda est, quia maxime nocet. cum excogitasset deus duorum sexuum rationem, adtribuit iis ut se inuicem adpeterent et coniunctione gauderent. itaque ardentissimam cupiditatem cunctarum animantium corporibus admiscuit, ut in hos adfectus auidissime ruerent eaque ratione propagari et multiplicari genera possent. quae cupiditas et adpetentia in homine uehementior et acrior inuenitur, uel quia hominum multitudinem uoluit esse maiorem uel quoniam uirtutem soli homini dedit, ut esset laus et gloria in coercendis uoluptatibus et abstinentia sui. scit ergo aduersarius ille noster quanta sit uis huius cupiditatis, quam quidam necessitatem dicere maluerunt, eamque a recto et bono ad prauum et malum transfert. inlicita enim desideria inmittit, ut aliena contaminent quibus habere propria sine delicto licet. obicit quippe oculis inritabiles formas suggeritque fomenta et uitiis pabulum subministrat; tum in intimis uisceribus stimulos omnes conturbat et commouet et naturalem illum incitat atque inflammat ardorem, donec inretitum hominem inplicatumque decipiat. ac ne quis esset qui poenarum metu abstineret alieno, lupanaria quoque constituit et pudorem infelicium mulierum publicauit, ut ludibrio haberet tam eos qui faciunt quam quas pati necesse est. his obscenitatibus animas ad sanctitatem genitas uelut in caeni gurgite demersit, pudorem extinxit, pudicitiam flagitauit. idem etiam mares maribus adplicuit et nefandos coitus contra naturam contraque institutum dei machinatus est. sic imbuit homines et armauit ad nefas omne. quid enim potest esse sanctum us qui aetatem inbecillam et praesidio indigentem libidini suae depopulandam foedandamque sunstrauennt t non potest haec res pro magmtuaine scelens enarrari. nihil amplius istos appellare possum quam inpios et parricidas, quibus non sufficit sexus a deo datus, nisi etiam suum sexum profane ac petulanter inludant. haec tamen apud illos leuia et quasi honesta sunt. quid dicam de iis qui abominandam non libidinem, sed insaniam potius exercent? piget dicere, sed quid iis fore credamus quos non piget facere? et tamen dicendum est, quia fit: de istis loquor quorum teterrima libido et execrabilis furor ne capiti quidem parcit. quibus hoc uerbis aut qua indignatione tantum nefas prosequar? uincit officium linguae sceleris magnitudo. cum igitur libido haec edat opera et haec facinora designet, armandi aduersus eam uirtute maxima sumus. quisquis affectus illos frenare non potest, cohibeat eos intra praescriptum legitimi tori, ut et illut quod auide expetit consequatur et tamen in peccatum non incidat. nam quid sibi homines perditi nolunt? nempe honesta opera uoluptas sequitur: si ipsam per se adpetunt, iusta et legitima frui licet. quodsi aliqua necessitas probebit, tum uero maxime adhibenda uirtus erit, ut cupiditati continentia reluctetur. nec tantum alienis toris quaeque attingere non licet, uerum etiam publicis uulgatisque corporibus abstinendum deus praecipit docetque nos, cum duo inter se corpora fuerint copulata, unum corpus efficere.
pass_a_gloss: I come now to that pleasure which is perceived from touch: which sense is indeed of the whole body. But I think I must speak not about ornaments and clothes, but about lust alone, which must be most restrained, because it most harms. When God had thought out the reason of two sexes, He gave to them that they might strive for each other and rejoice in union. And so He mixed into the bodies of all living things a most ardent desire, so that they might rush into these affections most eagerly and for this reason the kinds might be propagated and multiplied. This desire and striving is found in man more vehement and sharp, either because He wanted there to be a greater multitude of men or because He gave virtue to man alone, so that there might be praise and glory in restraining desires and abstaining from them. Therefore, our adversary knows how great is the power of this desire, which some have preferred to call necessity, and he transfers it from what is right and good to what is wrong and evil. For he injects illicit desires, so that they might pollute what is alien, when it is permitted to have one's own without fault. He indeed throws before the eyes irresistible forms and suggests incitements and supplies nourishment to vices; then in the innermost bowels he stirs up all the goads and moves them and incites and inflames that natural ardor, until he deceives the man who is caught and entangled. And lest anyone should abstain from what is alien because of fear of punishments, he also established brothels and made public the shame of unhappy women, so that he might have as a mockery both those who do and those who must suffer. By these obscenities, he has submerged souls born for sanctity, as it were, in a whirlpool of mud, extinguished shame, and ravaged chastity. He has also joined males to males and devised unspeakable unions against nature and against God's institution. Thus, he has imbued men and armed them for every evil. What, indeed, can be holy for those who have handed over weak and defenseless age to their lust to be ravaged and defiled? This thing cannot be told as a great crime. I can call them nothing other than impious and parricides, for whom the sex given by God is not enough, unless they also profane and mock their own sex with wantonness. These things, however, are considered light and almost honorable among them. What shall I say about those who exercise not detestable lust, but rather insanity? It is distasteful to speak, but what shall we believe will happen to those who are not distasteful in doing? And yet it must be spoken, because it happens: I speak about those whose most foul lust and execrable fury does not even spare the head. With what words or what indignation shall I pursue so great a crime? The magnitude of the crime overcomes the duty of the tongue. When, therefore, this lust produces such works and designs such crimes, we must be armed with the greatest virtue against it. Whoever cannot restrain those affections, let him hold them within the bounds of the legitimate marriage bed, so that he may both attain what he eagerly seeks and yet not fall into sin. For what do lost men not want? Indeed, pleasure follows honest works: if they strive for it by itself, it is permitted to enjoy it justly and lawfully. But if some necessity proves it, then indeed virtue must be applied most, so that continence may resist desire. Nor is it only not permitted to touch the marriage beds of others, but also God teaches and instructs us to abstain from public and common bodies, when two bodies have been joined together, to make one body.

pass_b_english: I turn now to the pleasure that comes through touch, a sense that belongs to the whole body, but I will speak not of ornaments or clothing; I will speak of lust alone, because it must be restrained above all else, since it does the greatest harm.

When God had devised the rationale for the two sexes, He gave them a mutual longing and a joy in their union, and so He planted in the bodies of all living creatures a most ardent desire, so that they would rush eagerly into these affections and, for that reason, the kinds might be propagated and multiplied.

This desire and striving is found in human beings more vehement and keen, either because God willed a greater multitude of humankind or because He gave virtue to humanity alone, so that there would be praise and glory in restraining pleasures and in self‑abstinence.
Our adversary therefore knows well the power of this desire, which some have preferred to call necessity, and he twists it from what is right and good into what is wrong and evil.

He injects illicit desires so that they may defile what belongs to another, even though it is permitted to have one's own without fault; he parades irresistible forms before the eyes, suggests incitements, and supplies fuel to vices; then deep in the innermost parts he stirs up every goad, agitates them, kindles and inflames that natural ardor, until he deceives the man who has been snared and entangled.

And lest anyone should abstain from another's body out of fear of punishment, he also established brothels and exposed the shame of wretched women, so that he might hold up as a mockery both those who do the deed and those who are forced to suffer it.
By these obscenities he has plunged souls born for sanctity, as it were, into a whirlpool of mud, extinguished shame, and ravaged chastity.
He has joined males with males and contrived unspeakable unions contrary to nature and contrary to God's institution, and thus he has steeped men in wickedness and armed them for every evil.
What can be holy for those who hand over their weak and defenseless years to their lust to be ravaged and defiled? This crime cannot be described in terms adequate to its magnitude.

I can call them nothing but impious and parricides, for whom the sex given by God does not suffice, unless they also profane and wantonly mock their own sex; yet among them these things are regarded as light and almost honorable.
What shall I say of those who practice not detestable lust but sheer insanity? It revolts me to speak of it, but what do we suppose will become of those who feel no revulsion in doing it?

And yet it must be spoken, because it happens: I speak of those whose foulest lust and execrable fury does not spare even the head; with what words or what indignation shall I pursue so great a crime? The enormity of the crime silences the tongue.
Therefore, since this lust produces such works and designs such crimes, we must arm ourselves against it with the greatest virtue.
Whoever cannot restrain those affections must keep them within the bounds of the legitimate marriage bed, so that he may obtain what he eagerly seeks and yet not fall into sin.
For what do the lost not desire? Indeed, pleasure follows honorable works; if they pursue pleasure for its own sake, it is permitted to enjoy it justly and lawfully.
But if some necessity makes its claim, then virtue must be applied all the more, so that continence may resist desire.

Nor is it only forbidden to touch the marriage beds of others; God also commands and teaches us to abstain from public and common bodies, so that when two bodies have been joined together they become one body.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B are consistent with the source. The translation of 'legitimi tori' as 'legitimate marriage bed' (Pass A) and 'legitimate marriage bed' (Pass B) is a correct idiomatic rendering of the Latin metaphor. The translation of 'inretitum hominem inplicatumque' as 'the man who is caught and entangled' (Pass A) and 'the man who has been snared and entangled' (Pass B) preserves the sense. All clauses, including the complex descriptions of the adversary's actions and the moral distinctions regarding lust and insanity, are present.

The Latin text is accurately translated in Pass A and Pass B. The title 'The Dangers of Uncontrolled Desire' correctly reflects the content. All key terms such as 'uoluptas' (pleasure), 'tactus' (touch), 'libido' (lust), 'cupiditas' (desire), 'adpetentia' (striving), 'uirtus' (virtue), 'continentia' (continence), 'aduersarius' (adversary), 'deus' (God), 'institutum' (institution), and 'sanctitas' (sanctity) are consistently and accurately rendered. The inline citations are correctly matched to the quoted or alluded-to content. No omissions, additions, or distortions are found in the translation. The translation preserves the original meaning, including negation, agency, modality, and doctrine. The text is complete and faithful to the source.
